title: Update paths: USB, local Wi-Fi, remote Wi-Fi, and SD

spans.text: There are several ways to deliver firmware to a board. Choose based on whether you can reach the device, available networks and storage, and how it can recover after a failed update.

USB/Serial: the board is nearby and a cable uploads through its bootloader; simple, but not remote. Local Wi-Fi: ArduinoOTA or a device web updater is convenient on the same home/office network. Remote Wi-Fi: the device downloads a signed release from an HTTPS server; TLS alone does not prove that the firmware itself is trusted. SD card: carry the file to an offline device and install it locally. Bluetooth can transfer a file, but firmware updating needs a purpose-built transfer, boot/flash layout, integrity checks, and recovery code; it is not a universal ready-made Arduino/ESP32 OTA method.

A board without Wi-Fi, such as a classic UNO, cannot update itself over a network. An IDE upload over USB is not OTA. ESP32 A/B application slots can preserve a previous image across interrupted application updates, but that safety is not automatic for USB, SD, or every data partition.

spans.title: Important safety and compatibility note
spans.text: Check the exact board's flash layout for every method. Remote updates need version and cryptographic signature checks plus a recovery path for power loss.
